## Today's Goals {.smaller}

Today we will

- Perform additional data wrangling operations
  - Combining values from many columns (`unite`)
  - Separating values into many columns (`separate`)
  - Combining multiple data files (`bind_rows` and `bind_cols`)
- Reshape Data
  - Making data longer and narrower (`pivot_longer`)
  - Making data wider and shorter (`pivot_wider`)

We will use the **Parquet** version of the CRU data in

`AGNR-AREC280_Fall2026/Data/CRU/parquet`


## Create a Monthly CRU Data File

We will work on a monthly CRU data file

- Load data from the Parquet file
- The CRU data have multiple time levels
- Need to keep `Period` values of `JAN`,`FEB`, ...

What do we need to do?

## Create a Monthly CRU Data File

- Load the Parquet file
- Filter based on Period

```{r load_cru_tmp}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(arrow)

# Load the full fao dataset
read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"CRU","parquet","tmp_w_ISO3.parquet")
) |>
  filter(
    Period %in% c(
      "JAN","FEB","MAR","APR","MAY","JUN",
      "JUL","AUG","SEP","OCT","NOV","DEC"
    )
  )-> cru_tmp
```

## Displaying Loaded Data

```{r show_cru_tmp}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
glimpse(cru_tmp)
```


# Combining Columns

## Combining Data from Multiple Columns

- Sometimes information we want are spread across multiple columns
- We want to combine that info into a single column
- How can we do this in R?

. . .

```r
data |>
  unite(
  <new_colname>,
  <cols_to_combine>,
  sep="<separator>"
)
```

## Combine Columns in CRU

- CRU contains `Year` and `Period` columns
- Suppose you wanted a new text column named `MonthYear`
  - Contains `<month>-<year>`
  - e.g., `"JAN-2005"`
- How can you do that with `unite()`?
- Create this column and save it to your data frame

## Combine Columns in CRU - Result

```{r combine_cru_cols}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
cru_tmp |>
  unite(
    # New colname
    MonthYear,
    # Columns to combine
    c(Period,Year),
    # Separator
    sep="-"
  ) -> cru_tmp

glimpse(cru_tmp)
```

. . .

What happened to `Period` and `Year`?

## Combining Columns - Saving the originals

- By default, `unite()` removes the original columns it united
- You can override by setting `remove=FALSE`
- Technically not a destructive operation
- All the original data are still there!

What if we want it back?

# Separating data in columns

## Separating data in columns

- We have the month and year smashed together in a column
- What if we wanted separate `Year` and `Month` columns?
- There is additional text in the column
- A delimiter (separator)

```r
data |>
  separate(
    <col_to_separate>,
    <new_colnames>,
    sep="<separator>",
    remove=[TRUE|FALSE]
  )
```

## Separating a Combined Column

- Use the `separate()` verb to separate `MonthYear`
  - Separate `Year` and `Month` columns
  - Keep the `MonthYear` column
  
  
## Separating a column - Example

```{r separate_cru_tmp}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
cru_tmp |>
  separate(
    # Column to separate
    MonthYear,
    # New columns. Provided as text
    c("Month","Year"),
    # Separator
    sep="-",
    # Don't remove
    remove=FALSE
  )
```
Do you notice a problem with the new columns?

## Separating columns - Data Types

By default `separate` creates text (`<chr>`) columns

- In our original data `Year` is numeric
- We think of years as numeric
- What can we do?

. . .

- Convert after the fact using `mutate`
- Tell `separate` to attempt to convert columns with `convert=TRUE`

Let's do the latter

## Separating a column with Conversion

```{r convert_cru_tmp}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
cru_tmp |>
  separate(
    # Column to separate
    MonthYear,
    # New columns. Provided as text
    c("Month","Year"),
    # Separator
    sep="-",
    # Don't remove
    remove=FALSE,
    # Attempt to convert columns
    convert = TRUE
  ) -> cru_tmp

glimpse(cru_tmp)
```

## Other arguments to `separate()`

Separate has a few other important optional arguments

`extra="<warn|drop|merge>"`

- Determines how to handle cases where there are extra pieces to separate

`fill="<warn|left|right>"`

- Determines how to handle cases when there are too few pieces



# Combining data

## Combining Data from Multiple Data Frames

Think about **two** data frames that may contain similar information

- Separate files for different measurements (e.g., CRU)
- Separate files for different time periods
- Separate files for different places

## Tidyverse methods for combining data 

The tidyverse has several methods of combining data frames

- `bind_rows()` stacks rows of data frames
- `bind_cols()` stacks columns of data frames
- **Joins** use more complicated logic to match rows between datasets
  - Covered next week
  

## Stacking Rows

`bind_rows()` stacks rows of multiple data frames

- Each data frame is added to the bottom of the previous data frame
- Useful when you have multiple data frames with the same layout
  - Identical column names
  - Identical data types
- e.g., 
  - One data frame for each year of data
  - Otherwise identical


## Stacking Rows

`bind_rows()`

- Returns a single data frame, aligning columns by name
- Fills in with `NA` when a column doesn't exist

:::{.callout-warning}
### Watch out for inconsistent data types!

Each column needs a single data type. R will attempt to *coerce* values of each 
column to a single data type, but won't convert numbers to text or vice versa.
This can lead to unexpected `NA` values if you try to stack a column that 
switches between text and numeric data!

:::


## Two ways to use `bind_rows()`

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="45%" .text-left}
Just stack data frames

```r
bind_rows(data_2000,data_2001)





```

Stack rows from each data fame

But otherwise no way to tell them apart
:::

:::{.column width="10%" .text-right}

:::

:::{.column width="45%" .text-right}
Stack with identifier column

```r
bind_rows(
  list(
    "2000" = data_2000, 
    "2001" = data_2001
  ),
  .id="Year"
)
```

Adds a `Year` column with the corresponding
name from the `list()`

:::

::::


## Stacking Columns

`bind_cols()` stacks columns of multiple data frames

- Each data frame is added to the right of the previous data frame
- Useful when you have multiple data frames of information for the same observations
  - Observations align perfectly across each data frame
  - Column names do not overlap
- e.g., a wide table was split up into multiple files


## Stacking Columns

In general you won't use `bind_rows()`

- Few cases where you need to combine columns across data frames by matching rows
- Only useful when you have full knowledge of the provenance of each data frame, e.g., 
  - You intentionally split off columns from a data frame
  - Want to combine back later
- No checks for whether observations are correctly aligned
- Usually use **Joins** to match observations across dataframes (next week)


# Reshaping Data

## Reshaping Data Overview

What does it mean to reshape (pivot) data?

. . .

- Take information organized by columns and reorganize in rows or vice-versa
- Will change the *shape* of your data frame

**`pivot_longer()`**  

- New data are longer and narrower
- More rows, fewer columns
- Column information translated into rows


## Reshaping Data Overview

What does it mean to reshape (pivot) data?

**`pivot_wider()`**

- New data are wider and narrower
- More columns, fewer rows
- Row information is translated into columns

## Reshaping Data - The Old Way

- The pivot functions are relatively new
- The tidyverse previously used `gather` and `spread`
- They have the **superseded** lifecycle tag
- No new features will be added, but won't be removed soon
- Harder to use, Fewer features
- Avoid using them

# Pivoting Wider

## Using `pivot_wider()`

When you use `pivot_wider()` you should ask yourself three questions:

1. Which column(s) will **uniquely identify** observation in my new data frame? `id_cols`
1. Which column(s) contain information that will be used to construct new column names? `names_from`
1. Which column(s) contain values that will populate those new columns? `values_from`

Each answer tells you what to use for each of the required arguments!



## Example `pivot_wider()`

I would like to create a new version of the CRU data frame

- One row for each Country-Year
- Columns for the temperature in each month

How can I do this?


## Example `pivot_wider()`

- One row for each Country-Year
- Columns for the temperature in each month

1. Which column(s) will **uniquely identify** observation in my new data frame? `id_cols`
1. Which column(s) contain information that will be used to construct new column names? `names_from`
1. Which column(s) contain values that will populate those new columns? `values_from`

## Example `pivot_wider()`

- `id_cols = c(Year,Country)`
- `names_from = Period`
- `values_from = Value`

:::{.callout-warning}
### Remove extra columns before pivoting

When `pivot_wider()` rearranges your data frame it needs to know what to do with information
in each column. This is ambiguous for any column that doesn't show up in one of the 
three arguments. You should remove columns that aren't needed with `select()` before pivoting. 

:::

## Implement `pivot_wider()`

Reshape the CRU data to make month columns

- Remember to remove unneeded columns
- `id_cols = c(Year,Country)`
- `names_from = Month`
- `values_from = Value`



## Example `pivot_wider()`
```{r pivot_wider_cru}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
cru_tmp |>
  # Keep only columns needed for the pivot
  select(Year,Country,Month,Value) |>
  # Pivot to wider and shorter
  pivot_wider(
    # Columns that uniquely identify observations
    id_cols=c(Country,Year),
    # Column used to create names
    names_from=Month,
    # Column used to fill values
    values_from=Value
  ) -> cru_tmp_wide

glimpse(cru_tmp_wide)
```


# Visualizing the result

## Visualizing the result of `pivot_wider()`

Using the pivoted data

- Choose a single country
- Create a visualization
  - `Year` on the horizontal axis
  - A line plot of the January temperature in blue
  - A line plot of the July temperature in dark red
- Informative labels
- What is this visualization missing?


## Example visualization

```{r viz_1}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
# Filter to one country
cru_tmp_wide |>
  filter(Country == "Spain") -> cru_spain

ggplot(cru_spain,aes(x=Year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y=JAN),color="blue",linewidth=1) +
  geom_line(aes(y=JUL),color="red",linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x="Year",
    y="Average Temperature (C)",
    title="Seasonal Temperature by Year",
    subtitle="Spain"
  )
```

## Adding a manual legend

The visualization doesn't contain a legend

- R only creates a legend when you provide a `color` aesthetic
- Here color is a layer property
- To create a legend, you need to use aesthetics
- What goes in the aesthetic? **Data**
- What is the **data** that corresponds to the blue line? **"January"**

## Adding a manual legend

You can add a manual legend by

- Adding the `color` aesthetic to each layer
- Setting the `color` aesthetic value to the **label text** you want in the legend
- Using a scale color function to set the specific colors

## Adding a manual legend - Example

```{r viz_2}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
# Filter to one country
cru_tmp_wide |>
  filter(Country == "Spain") -> cru_spain

ggplot(cru_spain,aes(x=Year)) +
  # Add the legend text as the color aesthetic
  geom_line(aes(y=JAN,color="January"),linewidth=1) +
  geom_line(aes(y=JUL,color="July"),linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x="Year",
    y="Average Temperature (C)",
    title="Seasonal Temperature by Year",
    subtitle="Spain",
    color="Month"
  ) +
  # Discrete Viridis Scale
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Pivoting Longer

## Using `pivot_longer`

`pivot_longer` will make your data longer and narrower

- Converts information stored in columns to information stored in rows
- Effectively the reverse of `pivot_wider`

## `pivot_longer` Questions

Whenever you use `pivot_longer` ask yourself the following questions

1. Which column(s) do I want to transform (pivot)? `cols`
1. In what new column(s) should I put the names of these columns? `names_to`
1. In what new column(s) should I put the values from these columns? `values_to`

## Challenge - `pivot_longer`

Use `pivot_longer` on the wide dataframe we created earlier to undo the previous 
`pivot_wider`

:::{.callout-tip}
### Specifying columns in `pivot_longer`

The `cols` argument may consist of many columns. In this example it's all 12 month
names. You can use the tidy-select syntax to save yourself typing.

You want to pivot everything except `Year` and `Country` so you could use

`cols=-c(Year,Country)`

Alternatively, the month names are 3 capital letters and you can match each with a 
[Regular Expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression) and the `matches`
tidy-select function

`cols=matches("^[A-Z]{3}$")`
:::

## Challenge - `pivot_longer`

1. Ask yourself the three questions in the previous slide
1. Use answers to construct the arguments 
1. Use `pivot_longer` to transform the data frame
1. Compare it to the original. Has anything changed?

## Solution - `pivot_longer`

```{r cru_longer}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
cru_tmp_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols=matches("^[A-Z]{3}$"),
    names_to="Month",
    values_to="Value"
  )
```
